rationale: Start with a broad, mid-strength scouting gradient at moderate temperature to maximize the chance all 10 compounds elute within 42 min while giving a first view of the retention window and critical pairs.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only available gain is reducing t_last. Shorten the gradient one step while keeping composition range and temperature fixed to test how much run time can be cut before any pair drops below baseline target resolution.

The method is still fully resolved and only slightly above the 10 min penalty threshold, so shorten the gradient one more step to try to bring the last peak under 10 min while monitoring the known critical pair around peaks 6 and 7.

At 14 min the run is fast enough, but the critical pair just fell below 1.5. Lowering temperature one step should selectively increase retention and often improve selectivity/resolution with only a modest increase in t_last, potentially reaching a perfect score.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity, so test the opposite direction. Raising T one step may improve the critical mid-run selectivity enough to push the weakest pair above 1.5 while likely keeping the last peak under 10 min.

Temperature changes hurt selectivity, so keep 40 C and instead make the gradient slightly shallower by lowering phi1 one step. This should increase separation in the crowded mid-region while likely keeping the last peak below 10 min.

A perfect CRF has been reached, so now optimize for a shorter run while preserving full resolution. Shortening the gradient by one step is the most direct way to test whether the critical pair remains at or above 1.5 with a faster method.

tG 12 was too aggressive, so return to 14 min and tighten the gradient window another step by lowering phi1. That should keep full resolution and may pull t_last just under 10 min for a more robust perfect-scoring method than the current borderline 10.01 min result.

The best current method is essentially optimal but sits right at the 10 min cutoff, so probe whether a cooler temperature can retain the favorable selectivity from phi1 0.85 while shifting the last peak slightly earlier or at least revealing the temperature trend near the optimum.

Use the known optimum composition window and temperature, but lengthen the gradient one step to create a more robust fully resolved method with extra margin on the critical pair. This checks how much selectivity reserve exists around the optimum for later fine-tuning of phi0 if needed.

The optimum seems to lie at 14 min, 40 C, phi1 0.85, so now test whether widening the window slightly at the low-organic end improves the critical mid-run selectivity without pushing the last peak past 10 min. Changing phi0 can shift early/mid spacing differently from changing phi1 or tG.

Probe phi0 in the opposite direction around the perfect method. Raising phi0 may shift the crowded middle slightly earlier and could trim t_last below 10 min while revealing whether the critical pair tolerates a narrower low-end window.

The higher phi0 improved on the earlier perfect method, so continue in that direction to see whether the run can be shortened further while preserving the critical pair above 1.5. This tests whether phi0 0.15 is the local optimum or whether more compression of the low-end window is beneficial.

phi0 0.15 looks near-optimal, so now test whether lowering phi1 one step can keep full resolution while reducing overall retention enough to improve practical speed. This maps the local neighborhood around the current best method without changing the successful temperature or gradient time.

The best region is centered at phi0 0.15, tG 14, T 40, and lowering phi1 made the run slightly too long. Test phi1 one step higher instead to see whether stronger ending solvent preserves the critical pair while giving an even faster fully resolved method.

The local optimum is clear, so use one remaining exploratory point to see whether a shorter gradient can be rescued by lower temperature at the improved phi0 0.15 setting. If this restores the critical pair above 1.5 while keeping t_last under 10 min, it could reveal an equally perfect but faster method.

Complete the local test at the faster 12 min gradient by checking the opposite temperature direction. If higher temperature rescues the critical pair at phi0 0.15 better than lower temperature did, it could identify a faster perfect method; otherwise it confirms 14 min as the true limit.

Since 12 min is clearly too short, use the remaining budget to map whether temperature at the successful 14 min, phi0 0.15, phi1 0.85 condition reveals any hidden selectivity advantage. This colder endpoint will confirm whether 40 C is truly optimal around the best method.

Cold temperatures are clearly detrimental, so test one warmer point around the best composition to complete the local temperature map at the successful 14 min gradient. This will confirm whether 40 C is indeed the selectivity optimum for the critical pair near peaks 6 and 7.

One final warm-point check will define how sharply selectivity degrades above 40 C around the best method. This is mainly confirmatory, but could still expose an unexpected order/selectivity change near the temperature limit.

The 55 C run came surprisingly close to full resolution with a much shorter retention window, so test the upper temperature limit once. A selectivity crossover could conceivably restore all pairs to at least 1.5 while keeping the run very fast.

With only a few injections left, test the one remaining likely route to a faster perfect method: combine the improved phi0 0.15 with a shorter 12 min gradient and lower phi1 to recover some selectivity. If this fails, injection 12 remains the clear best practical choice.

A narrower window at phi1 0.80 increased resolution but slightly delayed the last peak, so test one more step lower in phi1 at the proven 14 min gradient. This may reveal whether the critical-pair gain continues enough to maintain a perfect score with acceptable t_last, or whether phi1 0.85 remains the optimum.

The remaining unexplored local direction is a stronger final composition at the best phi0, tG, and T. Since phi1 0.90 was close but slightly under-resolved, this tests whether a further selectivity shift occurs at the high end that could restore full resolution while keeping the run very fast.

Use the final shot on the only promising untested neighborhood left: the perfect phi1 0.85, tG 14 window with the lower phi0 that previously gave the strongest critical-pair margin, combined with a moderate temperature increase rather than the more extreme changes that failed elsewhere. It is a long shot, but could preserve full resolution while moving the last peak earlier than the current best perfect method.
